stated: Introduce a carbon tax on all fossil fuels, whether produced or imported, proportional to greenhouse gas emissions. The tax would start at £120 per tonne and rise to £500 per tonne within ten years, designed to incentivise decarbonisation.

source.quote: Elected Greens will advocate for a carbon tax to incentivise businesses to decarbonise their supply chains and to help raise the money needed to shift to a zero-carbon economy. Elected Greens will propose levying a carbon tax at an initial rate of £120 per tonne, rising to a maximum of £500 per tonne of carbon emitted within ten years. This is deliberately designed to make it cheaper for the emitter to take steps to reduce emissions rather than pay the tax.

bearing_set.reason: The policy's entire mechanism is a rising price on fossil-fuel emissions designed to drive decarbonisation — it directly targets the emissions trajectory fundamental earns a real verdict.

A tax starting at £120/tonne rising to £500/tonne on all fossil fuels would materially raise household energy bills, fuel and heating costs, and prices throughout supply chains — a non-negligible cost-of-living effect, especially for lower-income households.

Carbon taxes have well-documented regressive incidence: lower-income households spend a higher share of income on energy and fuel, so absent progressive recycling of revenue the gap between richest and rest widens — a direct inequality effect.
A tax at £120–£500/tonne across all fossil fuels would generate very substantial public revenue, materially affecting whether spending is funded or borrowed and the sustainability of the debt path.

A carbon tax at this magnitude significantly raises energy costs for businesses and shifts investment patterns; near-term competitiveness and output face downward pressure, while long-term living standards could gain through avoided climate damage and clean-energy productivity — a genuine dual-horizon prosperity effect.

membership_note: Five fundamentals earn real verdicts: O6 is the primary design target; O2 and O14 capture the household price and distributional burdens; O12 captures the large revenue effect; O13 captures the contested near-term vs long-term prosperity trade-off. O11 (income tax burden) is not included because the household cost effect routes cleanly through O2 (prices of essentials) rather than through take-home pay from earnings. O4 and O10 are not included as any labour-market or freedom effects are insufficiently direct to clear the non-negligible bar independently of O13 and O2.
